title: A statistical explanation of visual space
research_question: To determine whether the differences between real and apparent distances in human visual perception could be explained by the statistical relationship of scene geometry and the observer, based on the probability distribution of physical distances in natural scenes.

participants.description: Data points from a database of natural scene geometry acquired via laser range scanning, representing physical locations in typical outdoor visual environments.
participants.recruitment: Laser range scanning of 10 natural scenes in Durham, North Carolina, USA, generating 512x512 pixel range images.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Natural outdoor scenes (e.g., fields, forests, buildings) captured as 3D range images. The laser scanner was mounted on a tripod at 1.65 m above ground, acquiring 512x512 pixel images covering 326° horizontally and 70° vertically.

measures.construct: Physical distance, elevation, and azimuth of locations in natural scenes
measures.instrument: Laser range scanner (Riegl USA Inc. LMS-Z210 3D Laser Scanner)

measures.construct: Probability distributions of physical distances and distance differences
measures.instrument: Statistical analysis of range image data
Bayesian optimal observer model (local mass mean of probability distribution multiplied by Gaussian likelihood function)

findings.antecedent: Probability distribution of radial distances from the observer to physical locations in natural scenes
findings.consequent: Perceived distance of objects in impoverished settings (specific distance tendency)
findings.mechanism: In the absence of distance cues, perceived distance is biased toward the most probable physical distance in typical visual scenes, which has a maximum at about 3 m.
findings.quote: this distribution has a maximum probability at about 3 m. The agreement... is thus consistent with a probabilistic explanation of the 'specific distance tendency'.

findings.antecedent: Probability distribution of differences in physical distances between two locations in natural scenes (especially with small angular separations)
findings.consequent: Perceived relative distance of neighboring objects (equidistance tendency)
findings.mechanism: In the absence of information about distance differences, perceived relative distances are biased toward the most probable difference, which is near zero for nearby objects.
findings.quote: As the distribution between two locations with relatively small angular separations... has a maximum near zero, any two neighboring objects should be perceived to be at about the same distance from the observer.

findings.antecedent: Probability distribution of physical distances at eye level in natural scenes
findings.consequent: Perceived distance of near objects (overestimated) and far objects (underestimated) at eye level
findings.mechanism: Perceived distance is a linear function of physical distance, biased by the prior distribution of distances at eye level, leading to overestimation for near objects and underestimation for far objects, with a crossover point at approximately 5-6 m.
findings.quote: the distance that should be perceived on this basis is approximately a linear function of physical distance, with near distances being overestimated and far distances underestimated

findings.antecedent: Probability distribution of physical distances of points at different elevation angles relative to the horizontal plane at eye level
findings.consequent: Perceived location of objects on the ground (closer and higher than physical position)
findings.mechanism: The statistical characteristics of distance as a function of elevation angle (e.g., average ground surface being curved and increasingly inclined toward the observer) bias perceived locations to be closer and higher.
moderators_reported: declination of the line of sight
findings.quote: The apparent location of an object predicted by the probability distributions in Fig. 5 is increasingly higher and closer to the observer as the declination of the line of sight decreases

findings.antecedent: Local dip in the ground plane (physical locations at elevations within [-30.8°, -26.8°] were at least 0.15 m below ideal ground)
findings.consequent: Perceived distance of objects on the ground
findings.mechanism: A local dip in the ground shifts the probability distribution of horizontal distances toward greater distances, leading to an overestimation of perceived distance (0.2-0.6 m).
findings.quote: the probability distribution of horizontal distances shifts toward greater distances when the ground dips locally... The expected overestimation when the terrain deviates negatively from a more or less flat ground plane is about 0.2-0.6 m

findings.antecedent: Local hump in the ground plane (physical locations at elevations within [-30.8°, -26.8°] were at least 0.15 m above ideal ground)
findings.consequent: Perceived distance of objects on the ground
findings.mechanism: A local hump in the ground shifts the probability distribution of horizontal distances toward smaller distances, leading to an underestimation of perceived distance (0.1-0.5 m).
findings.quote: when there is positive deviation in the ground plane, the probability distribution shifts toward smaller horizontal distances... perceived distance in the presence of a local hump should be slightly but consistently underestimated (by 0.1-0.5 m)

mechanisms: The characteristics of human visual space are determined statistically according to the probability distributions of the possible stimulus sources.
Visual systems have evolved to take advantage of statistical structure, or probabilistic information, in generating perceptions of physical space.

A probabilistic strategy can be formalized in terms of Bayesian 'optimal observer theory', where perceived distance is biased by the prior probability distribution of physical distances underlying visual stimuli.
The inherent ambiguity of visual stimuli (infinite possible physical sources for a given retinal projection) necessitates a probabilistic strategy for generating perceptions of distance.
moderators: Presence of additional information pertinent to distance
implementation_implications: Understanding the statistical properties of natural visual environments is crucial for explaining apparent distance and the structure of visual space.
limitations: The paper does not explicitly list limitations of its own method or data, but rather emphasizes the necessity of its probabilistic approach to explain the complexity of visual perception. It critiques other theories for not accounting for the statistical properties of natural visual environments.
